The thirty-seven factors [of enlightenment] have the mind as their essential nature.
This mind has three levels.
The first is the consciousness of phenomena (vastu-vijñāna),
which refers to the six consciousnesses;
within this, they perceive that there are dharmas external to the mind.
There is a mind outside of dharmas;
this mind discriminates and observes external objects as the contemplation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa).
Second is deluded consciousness.
This refers to the seven consciousnesses.
Apart from these, there is no phenomenon outside the center of the mind;
all dharmas are manifested from the deluded thoughts of one's own mind.
It is like what is seen in a dream;
within the phenomena manifested by one's own mind, one investigates and contemplates them as the contemplation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa).
Third is true consciousness (tathatā-vijñāna).
That is to say:
among the eight consciousnesses,
there is no phenomenon apart from this central mind.
Outside of phenomena there is no mind;
mind and the dharma-realm are of one substance, though their meanings are distinguished.
Because they are of one substance, the mind subsumes all phenomena.
All things are dharmas within a single mind.
According to the divisions of these dharmas, the mind extensively manifests as many minds as there are atoms in the dharma-realm.
This mind has never been obstructed by those dharmas from the very beginning.
That which is described as "concealment" refers to false defilement;
to cause this false defilement to cease and to inwardly illuminate the true nature is called the contemplation of the factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣya*).
Within that Hīnayāna, there exists only the initial gateway of the contemplation of the phenomenal consciousness (*vṛtti-vijñāna*).
These are explained as the factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣya*).
In the Mahāyāna teachings, first there is the contemplation of phenomena (*vastu-vipaśyanā*),
followed by the contemplation of false consciousness (*vikalpa-jñāna*) which involves the destruction of the marks of emotional attachment.
The subsequent cessation of deluded thoughts constitutes the contemplation of true consciousness.
Such is the essential nature [of these states]. These two gates are concluded.
Next, the third gate discusses their differences based on permanence and impermanence.
Because that which is cultivated in the Hīnayāna takes as its essence the mind-consciousness characterized by beginningless and endless impermanence and arising-and-ceasing,
the Mahāyāna is not like this;
it begins with the cultivation of impermanence.
Ultimately, this becomes permanent.
Since the perfected state takes the true mind as its essence, these three gates are concluded.
Next, the differences [between the teachings] will be explained by means of the categories of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
The factors of the path in the Hīnayāna encompass both the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
The first twenty-two, which exist prior to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*),
are termed "outflow-tainted."
The seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold path, when situated on the path of seeing,
are termed "untainted" (anāsrava).
The initial cultivation undertaken by a bodhisattva, however, is tainted (sāsrava).
Since it ultimately accomplishes all that is untainted (*anāsrava*),
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) are proclaimed within *nirvāṇa* as the pure holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
"If even tainted wholesome dharmas can serve as causes for untainted dharmas,
why cannot they be called pure brahmacarya?"
The Buddha said:
"Because the nature of that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is inverted, it is not the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Because the nature of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is without outflows (*anāsrava*), they are the holy life."
Based on this corroboration, it is clearly understood that these will ultimately result in all untainted [dharmas]. This concludes the four gates.
Next, we shall proceed to demonstrate the differences by examining the mind as a condition.
The Path is of two kinds:
first, that which is cultivated through conditions;
second, that which is realized in reality.
The wisdom of discernment that contemplates objects to break through fetters is called "contemplative treatment" (*yuan-zhi*).
The cessation of contemplation wherein the true mind manifests, the passions subside, and one accords with suchness in immovability is called "actual realization" (*shi-zheng*).
In the teachings of the Hīnayāna, there is only the cultivation of counteractive conditions (*pratipakṣa*) and a complete absence of actual realization;
it is not so in the Mahāyāna, which,
from the very beginning of its practice, employs the cultivation of counteractive conditions as the skillful means for entering the path.
Ultimately, these are realized as the true path; this concludes the five gates.
Next, their differences are clarified according to their depth and shallowness.
The teachings and practices of the Śrāvakas differ accordingly.
The path and practice discussed in the Abhidharma are extremely shallow,
consisting merely of the contemplation of the Four Truths and the sixteen aspects of the noble ones.
What is elucidated in the *Tattvasiddhi* is the contemplation of the Four Truths alone as being empty of intrinsic nature, their names and functions being merely provisional designations.
The bodhisattva, in practicing, does not grasp at the mark of existence regarding all phenomena;
does not grasp at the mark of non-existence;
and does not grasp at the marks of both existence and non-existence, nor neither existence nor non-existence.
Because one realizes, as it truly is, the equality of the ultimate meaning that transcends verbal expression,
the *Bhūmivastu* asks:
"What are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment of the Mahāyāna?"
The bodhisattva does not give rise to false conceptualizations regarding the body,
nor does he grasp at any non-existent nature.
He understands, as it truly is, the ultimate reality that transcends verbal expression.
As it is with the mindfulness of the body, so it is with the remaining foundations of mindfulness and all other factors of the path;
these are called the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment of the Mahāyāna.
The non-arising of false appearances clarifies the departure from existence.
Not grasping at non-existence and not clinging to nothingness—
this clarifies the meaning of being free from characteristics and free from verbal expression;
it is the true nature of phenomena known as it truly is.
What Nāgārjuna has taught is also the same as this; thus ends the section on these six gates.
Next, the differences are revealed by means of the coarse and the subtle.

Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) practiced by the Śrāvakas, they are only able to know coarsely the five faculties, the five objects, and non-manifest form (*avijñaptirūpa*), but not subtly.
The Bodhisattva knows the body as being like the distinct colors of the atoms within the dharma-realm;
this is beyond the reach of the followers of the Two Vehicles.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
That which is described within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is known through wisdom;
its differentiation as form is immeasurable and boundless,
and is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
I did not explain this at all in that sutra. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* also states:
"A bodhisattva is able to practice the contemplation of the body as being an immeasurable locus of skillful means."
As it is with the foundation of mindfulness of the body, so it is with the other foundations of mindfulness and other paths.
For the śrāvaka, observing them collectively is termed "coarse," whereas for the bodhisattva, knowing them individually is said to be "subtle. This concludes the seven gates.
Next, regarding the differences in the cultivation of practice,
there are two distinct meanings within the Hīnayāna teachings. First, as for the differences in conduct,
one trains separately in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment through distinct modes of mental attention (*manasikāra*), each of which arises individually.
First, regarding succession, they cannot exist simultaneously.
Second, even when occurring simultaneously, the mind and its mental factors (citta-caitta) are distinguished according to their respective functions.
Because the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) apprehend different objects, they cannot occur simultaneously; they must proceed one after another.
The others are acquired simultaneously.
For this reason, within the stage of the first dhyāna, thirty-four categories arise all at once.
Among those four foundations of mindfulness, one arises as the primary focus while the others are present in a latent manner; when combined, these constitute thirty-four categories.
The remaining three foundations of mindfulness arise separately before and after [the first dhyāna].
In the future, thirty-three categories of the second dhyāna arise simultaneously;
among the thirty-four categories of the preceding first dhyāna, "joy" (prīti) is excluded from the future.
In the second dhyāna, initial application (vitarka) is excluded;
the rest are all similar.
In that intermediate dhyāna, as well as in the third and fourth dhyānas, thirty-two factors arise simultaneously.
Among the thirty-four factors of the aforementioned first dhyāna, with the exception of joy (*prīti*) and applied thought (*vitarka*),
the remainder are all similar. In the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness, twenty-nine categories arise simultaneously.
Among the thirty-four factors of the aforementioned first dhyāna, excluding joy, applied thought, and the three types of precepts,
the remainder are all similar.
In the realm of desire and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nineteen path-factors arise simultaneously.
The four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, and one type [of application] arising from among the foundations of mindfulness—
this constitutes nineteen.
Such is the system of the Hīnayāna.
Within the Mahāyāna teachings, there are likewise two kinds:
first, the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment through distinct mental applications at the initial stage;
second, the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment through their simultaneous and sudden arising at the matured stage.
Therefore, the *Dìjīng* (Sutra on the Grounds) states:
"The Bodhisattva, in every thought-moment, is fully endowed with all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
In every thought-moment, he brings them forth clearly and simultaneously, not sequentially. This concludes the eight gates.
Next, the differences between the Great and Small Vehicles are clarified;
this may also be termed a difference in the practice of benefiting others.
What is cultivated by the Hīnayāna is biased toward self-benefit, with no broad concern for others.
It is termed "small.
That which is cultivated by a bodhisattva benefits both self and others;
because it is practiced through such universal benefit, it is designated as "great."
Therefore, the *Dìjīng* (Earth Sūtra) states:
"Not abandoning sentient beings while practicing the factors of enlightenment is called 'protecting the Hīnayāna. This concludes the nine gates.
Next, the differences between the Great and Small Vehicles in their methods for treating hindrances are clarified.
That which is cultivated by the Śrāvakas only severs the four abodes [of afflictions] and cannot exhaust them completely;
that practiced by the Bodhisattvas severs all five abodes, while simultaneously pacifying and counteracting the conditions [that give rise to them].
Because it is profound and vast, these ten gates are hereby concluded.
Next, the differences in the attainment of fruits between the Great and Small Vehicles are explained.
That which is cultivated by the Hīnayāna results only in the fruits of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha.
The practices of a bodhisattva can attain the fruit of Buddhahood;
furthermore, the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) by those of the Hīnayāna attains the fruit of skillful means,
but does not attain intrinsic purity (prakṛti-viśuddhi).
The practices of the Mahāyāna fully attain the fruit of the purity of nature through skillful means.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment can serve as the cause for the non-arising of afflictions."
It also serves as the efficient cause for nirvāṇa;
through the skillful means of awakening, it eliminates obstructions and severs defilements,
enabling afflictions to never arise again.
This Path is able to give rise [to it];
therefore, it acts as the generative cause for it.
The Path is able to manifest the inherently pure nirvana.
Therefore, for their sake, they act as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
The distinction between the great and the small is thus briefly explained.
The foregoing concludes the general explanation of the meaning of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya-dharma*).
Within the second section, the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) are explained individually.
First, the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are explained.
This is because the four foundations of mindfulness destroy the four inversions and open the gateway to the true nature of reality; therefore, they are analyzed first.
Furthermore, among the factors of enlightenment, wisdom is the primary factor.
Since the foundations of mindfulness are themselves wisdom,
they are explained first.
Within this, there is a brief analysis by way of seven gates:
first, the explanation of the names and meanings; second, the distinction between the general and the specific;
third, the clarification of the differences among the three types of foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
Fourth, the distinction between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Fifth, the sequence of the treatise.
Sixth, the manifestation of the characteristics of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Seventh, explaining the text:
what are these names?
They are body, sensation, mind, and phenomena; these are the four.
The accumulation of form and shape is called the body (*kāya*).
That which experiences is termed sensation (*vedanā*).
That which is capable of cognition is called the mind (*citta*).
The intrinsic nature is called "dharma" (phenomenon).
That which guards the object is called "mindfulness" (smṛti).
The four bases, such as the body and so forth, which are the locations where mindfulness arises, are called "foundations of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna). This concludes this section.
Next, the general and specific [applications] are discussed.
In principle, all phenomena (*dharmas*) without exception can serve as both general and specific foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
For now, however, we shall explain them generally and specifically with reference to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
To distinguish the five aggregates and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) as the four foundations of mindfulness is called "distinctive" (*pṛthak*).
To take the five aggregates and unconditioned phenomena collectively as the object is called the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*).
The "eye" serves as the general category;
what are its specific characteristics?
The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) constitutes the body.
The aggregate of sensation is "feeling";
the aggregate of consciousness is "mind";
and the aggregates of perception and mental formations, together with the three unconditioned phenomena, combined constitute "dharmas."
Since the aggregates (skandhas) already number five,
and since [the bases] are obtained by relying on the contemplation of the feet,
why labor to provide a fourfold explanation?
The dharmas of the aggregates (skandha) are indeterminate in their opening and closing;
in summary, they are all but one: conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma).
Alternatively, they may be divided into two.
There are only name and form.
The four aggregates are called "name," and the aggregate of form is called "form."
Alternatively, they may be divided into three,
namely the three cultivations,
as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
That is to say:
regarding the body, precepts, and mind—
within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), the five sense faculties are designated as "body."
Restraint is called cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The two karmas of body and speech are explained as being the precepts (*śīla*).
The four aggregates are called mind (*citta*).
Furthermore, it is also said that afflictions, karma, and suffering are distinct,
and these likewise constitute three.
Alternatively, they are said to be four.
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, the four nutriments, the four stations of consciousness,
and so forth, as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
how is it that the aggregates (*skandha*) are divided into the four nutriments?
Within the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) is taught;
consciousness (vijñāna) is taught as the food of consciousness (vijñāna-āhāra);
and within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha), volition (cetanā) and contact (sparśa) are taught.
Setting aside perception and feeling,
the remaining aggregates— excluding consciousness itself— are the bases for consciousness;
these are called the four stations of consciousness (*catvāraḥ vijñānasthitayaḥ*).
Alternatively, they are divided into five,
which are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Alternatively, they are divided into six.
The five aggregates and the formations dissociated from mind are sometimes described as twelve;
"twelve" refers to the twelve bases (āyatana) and the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
Some speak of eighteen,
namely,
the eighteen elements (dhātus).
Alternatively, twenty-two faculties (indriya) may be taught;
thus, they are not limited to a single enumeration.
For now, based on one approach, they are provisionally divided into four types.
Based on this, one gives rise to contemplation in order to destroy the four inversions;
therefore, only four are mentioned.
Permanence, bliss, self, and purity constitute these four inversions.
Ordinary worldlings mostly conceive of purity within form,
pleasure within sensation,
and permanence within the mind.
One establishes the existence of a self within all phenomena such as perception and mental formations.
To destroy this view, one contemplates the impurity of form to eliminate the inversion of purity,
and contemplates sensation as suffering to eliminate the inversion of pleasure.
Contemplating the impermanence of the mind destroys the inversion of permanence;
contemplating the selflessness of phenomena destroys the inversion of self.
Such are their distinct characteristics.
What are the general characteristics?
There are six broad explanations.
First, one generally contemplates the five aggregates and unconditioned phenomena as suffering, impermanent, empty, non-self, and so forth.
Second, one contemplates the five aggregates and unconditioned phenomena as a whole through the four truths and the sixteen noble practices.
Third, one contemplates the five aggregates and unconditioned phenomena as a whole, recognizing them as being nominally designated, devoid of intrinsic nature, empty, and quiescent.
Fourth, one universally contemplates that the five aggregates and unconditioned phenomena are false conceptualizations, devoid of marks, empty, and quiescent.
Fifth, one universally contemplates that the five aggregates and unconditioned phenomena are all illusory conceptualizations appearing within the mind, ultimately being non-existent dharmas.

Sixth, observing the five aggregates and unconditioned phenomena (*asamskṛta-dharma*) as a whole, one perceives that their true nature is the collection of dharmas and that their fundamental essence is eternally quiescent.
Within the first gate, the observation of suffering and impermanence is restricted to the five aggregates.
The contemplation of emptiness and non-self penetrates unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
For now, let us examine it by way of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
This contemplation is difficult to accomplish; it is achieved through gradual cultivation. Within this, there are twenty distinct gateways of contemplation.
Within the five aggregates, there are ten gateways consisting of pairwise combinations.
The first gateway is the combined contemplation of form and feeling;
the second gateway is the combined contemplation of form and perception.
The third gate consists of the combined contemplation of form and formations;
the fourth gate consists of the combined contemplation of form and consciousness.
Having removed the aggregate of form, [the same applies].
The combined contemplation of sensation and perception is the fifth gate.
The combined contemplation of sensation and formations is the sixth gate.
The combined contemplation of sensation and consciousness is the seventh gate.
Excluding form and excluding feeling,
the combined contemplation of perception and formations constitutes the eighth gate;
the combined contemplation of perception and consciousness constitutes the ninth gate.
Excluding form, feeling, and perception,
the combined contemplation of formations and consciousness constitutes the tenth gate.
There are six gates consisting of the combined contemplation of three [factors] at a time.
Form, feeling, and perception are combined and contemplated as one;
form, perception, and mental formations are combined as the second;
and form, mental formations, and consciousness are combined as the third.
Excluding the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the combination of feeling, perception, and formations constitutes the fourth.
The combination of feeling, formations, and consciousness constitutes the fifth.
Excluding form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, their combination constitutes the sixth.
Including these with the preceding ones, they form a total of sixteen.
There are three ways to combine the contemplation of the four [aggregates] into groups of four:
first, combining the contemplation of form, feeling, perception, and formations as one; [the other two follow].
Contemplating form together with perception, mental formations, and consciousness constitutes two.
Excluding the aggregate of form,
contemplating feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness together constitutes three.
Including the preceding [sixteen], there are nineteen.
These nineteen gates are called the "General Expedient Means.
Furthermore, the combined contemplation of the five aggregates is treated as one.
Including the preceding ones, there are twenty.
This subsequent section is named "Accomplishment through General Mindfulness" (*sāmānyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
This particular cycle corresponds precisely to the general mindfulness meditation (*sāmānyasmṛtyupasthāna-vipaśyanā*) of the Abhidharma.

Regarding the second gate: one contemplates the five aggregates (*skandha*) and the dharma of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) collectively as the Four Noble Truths and the sixteen aspects of the noble path (*āryākāra*).
One contemplates those aggregates of outflow (*āsrava*) within birth and death as the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Within that, specifically contemplating [the aggregates] as suffering, impermanent, empty,
and non-self constitutes the four modes of practice.
Contemplating those five aggregates, which are the causal formations of birth and death, constitutes the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Within that, specifically observing the cause, the accumulation, and the condition constitutes four further modes of practice;
together with the preceding ones, there are eight.
One observes the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) as the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
Within that, the specific contemplation of the path as a vehicle like a track further comprises four practices;
together with the preceding ones, there are twelve.
One contemplates that unconditioned phenomenon of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Within this, there are four further modes of practice— namely, cessation (*nirodha*), tranquility (*śānta*), excellence (*praṇīta*), and emergence (*niḥsaraṇa*)— which,
when added to the preceding sixteen, constitute the total.
This gateway corresponds to all meditative practices from the stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) upward within the Abhidharma system.
Because that is collectively termed the "contemplation of mindfulness of dharmas" (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).

As for the third gate: the comprehensive contemplation of the five aggregates and unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma), which employs provisional designations, is termed the conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya).
The emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*) and quiescence is taken as the ultimate truth;
this meaning is specifically discussed within the *Tattvasiddhi* (The Establishment of Reality).
As for the fourth gate, it consists of observing, in their entirety, the existence of the false appearances of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
That which is like an illusion, a city of Gandharvas, or a mirage in the heat of the sun is called the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
that which is signless, empty, and quiescent is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
This statement that "it is empty" means not only that it lacks intrinsic nature, but that even the characteristics of causes and conditions do not exist.
It is like the water of a mirage: from afar it appears to be near, yet upon close inspection, it is entirely non-existent.
Not only is there no intrinsic nature, but even water itself cannot be found;
all phenomena are like this.
This is the fifth gate.
Contemplating the five aggregates and unconditioned phenomena as a whole, one realizes that there are no phenomena external to the mind;
all arise from the deluded thoughts of one's own mind,
just as everything seen in a dream is created by the mind itself.

That which is called "worldly truth" (saṃvṛti-satya) refers to the fact that, when its essence is investigated to the limit, it is fundamentally non-existent; this is called "ultimate truth" (paramārtha-satya).
As for the sixth gate:
To contemplate those five aggregates and unconditioned phenomena as all being the true nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, integrated through dependent origination,
is called the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
To exhaustively investigate their fundamental nature and find that it is nothing other than True Suchness (tathatā) is the ultimate truth.
That which has been eternally quiescent and immovable from the very beginning is called the True Truth (*satya*).
These latter three gates are taught within the Mahāyāna,
whereas they are not discussed in the Hīnayāna.
These six are merely distinctions within the mindfulness of dharmas as a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). This concludes the two gateways.
Next, we shall discuss the distinctions among the three types of foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Regarding these "three types":
1. The foundation of mindfulness of intrinsic nature;
2. The foundation of mindfulness of common characteristics;
3. The foundation of mindfulness of objects.
The explanation has two sections:
first, the discernment of its characteristics;
second, the clarification of the distinction between severing and not severing hindrances.
Regarding the analysis of their characteristics, the intrinsic nature is discussed first.
In the Abhidharma system, it is taught that the four foundations of mindfulness have wisdom as their intrinsic nature.
If its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is wisdom (*prajñā*), why is it described as mindfulness (*smṛti*) in the sūtras?
It is called mindfulness because it follows after and accompanies mindfulness;
thus, by virtue of its association, it is said to be "with mindfulness."
Because the faculty of wisdom correctly apprehends phenomena without error,
it is called mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Furthermore, among the various mental factors, they serve as names for one another.
Just as the essence of the perception of superior form is actually wisdom,
yet it is called "perception," so too is this case.
Although its essence is wisdom (*prajñā*), it is designated as "mindfulness" (*smṛti*).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, in the beginning it is of the nature of mindfulness,
and in the end it is of the nature of wisdom.
Since this begins with the nature of mindfulness (*smṛti*), the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra), in its chapter on "Mental Factors" (*caitasika-dharma*), states:
"Just as a single application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) receives five names, namely:

application of mindfulness, faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*), factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*), and right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*)."
Because it is ultimately wisdom (*prajñā*), the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Wisdom arising from mindfulness that contemplates the body and so forth is called the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
In the Mahāyāna teachings, however, all virtues share a single essence, making it difficult to define them in isolation.
There is no harm in explaining it from the perspective of wisdom (*prajñā*).
As for the term "common mindfulness" (*samanvāhāra*),
its interpretation has three meanings.
First, regarding the object, it is said to be "shared.
Taking the body as the object,
all mental factors (*caitasika*) that arise therein, along with the concomitant morality (*śīla*), are collectively termed "mindfulness of the body" (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
The others are likewise.
Second, regarding the commonality of the distinct meanings based on the substance of practice:
within a single mindfulness of the body, all four foundations of mindfulness are fully present.
The precepts that arise accordingly are called mindfulness of the body;
feeling is the aggregate of sensation;
and the mental sovereign is the mind.
Wisdom and the other such factors are described as "dharmas.
Because these four applications of mindfulness are gathered together in one place,
they are called "conjoined" (sādhāraṇa).
The others are also like this.
Therefore, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* says:
"As the Blessed One has taught."
The accumulation of wholesome dharmas is called the "shared foundation of mindfulness" (*sādhāraṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*).
It is called "shared" because it arises from the three [foundations].
When wisdom contemplates the body, the wholesome dharmas that arise simultaneously and in association with that wisdom are likewise termed "mindfulness of the body."
The same applies to the others as well.
Wisdom is with-outflows (sāsrava);
all wholesome dharmas that arise concomitantly and accompany wisdom are likewise termed with-outflows.
The untainted [factors] are likewise.
All such cases are termed "shared" (sādhāraṇa) because they are identical to wisdom (prajñā).
Therefore, Nāgārjuna said:
"The path arising from causes and conditions—whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)—is likewise called the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
As for those that take the foundations of mindfulness as their object..."
There are two meanings of "understanding" (*prajñā*).
First, when the distracted mind universally takes all objects as its focus, it is called the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) through focusing.
The second [type] consists of the objects of focus that give rise to the mind of mindfulness; these are called the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Their meaning is similar to that of the term *prajñā* (wisdom), which in the sūtras is said to be synonymous with "knowing" (*jñāna*) and the "abode of wisdom" (*jñānasthāna*).
Furthermore, just as the arising of desire toward the five sense objects is called "desire," within this framework,
the objects of mindfulness of the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna) are indeterminate in their expansion and contraction;
in total, they are simply a single form (rūpa).
Alternatively, they may be divided into two:
namely, outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, they may also be divided into two based on whether they are determinate (*vyākṛta*), indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), retribution (*vipāka*), or non-retribution, and so forth.
Or it is explained as threefold:
first, that which is visible and resistant,
namely, form which is the objective domain of the eye and serves as the object for the eye.
That which is illuminated is called "visible.
Because it is opposed by and faces the physical sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*), it is called "resistant" (*sapratigha*).
Second, there are those that are invisible and resistant.
That is to say, the forms that are the objects of the ears, nose, tongue, and body,
but which are not seen by the eye faculty,
are called "invisible."
Those with resistance (*sapratigha*) are as previously described.
Three are invisible and non-resistant (*anidarśana-apratigha*):
namely, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) of wholesome and unwholesome [karma] that is the domain of the mind, as well as the matter of the five sense faculties.
That which is not perceived by the eye is called "invisible";
it is not that which is confronted by the physical sense organs through obstruction.
It is called "non-obstructive form" (apratigha-rūpa).
Alternatively, it is said to be fourfold,
namely the forms of the four great elements (mahābhūta-rūpa).
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"Form consists of the four great elements;
these four great elements are able to produce all kinds of form."
Subsuming the derivative from the fundamental, they are described as the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Furthermore, as established by Buddhadeva,
there are no distinct derived forms (*upādāyarūpa*) apart from the four great elements.
Therefore, four kinds are taught;
alternatively, six are taught,
namely the six objects of the sensory fields (ṣaḍviṣaya-rūpa).
The non-manifestation of good and evil, as well as the five faculties and material form, are collectively termed the dharma-object (dharmāyatana).
The remaining five [objects] may be understood accordingly.
Alternatively, ten types are taught.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*,
the five faculties and the five objects constitute these ten.
They do not mention them because, being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they manifest as the subtle and hidden characteristics of the body.
Alternatively, eleven [bases] are taught,
as stated in the Abhidharma:
the five faculties, the five objects, and within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), wholesome, unwholesome, and non-informative (avijñapti) phenomena.
If one follows the *Tattvasiddhi*, fourteen [elements] are taught:
the five faculties, the five objects, and the four great elements.
That treatise states:
The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the effects of the four sense objects (*viṣaya*).
Furthermore, they are the causes of the five sense organs (*indriya*) and the sense object of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*).
Because they are not subsumed within the [categories of] organs and objects, the great elements are explained separately.
In that school, non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is neither matter nor mind; therefore, it is not manifested as one of the aggregates (*skandha*).
In the *Abhidharma* system, since the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are tactile objects, they are not mentioned separately [as a distinct aggregate].
When subdivided, they are immeasurable.
These are taught as the objects of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Regarding the objects of mindfulness of feeling (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*), their classification is indeterminate;
in total, there is only a single feeling.
Alternatively, it is divided into two:
namely, body and mind.
That which is associated with the five consciousnesses and arises from the material sense-faculties is called "bodily sensation" (kāyikī vedanā).
That which is associated with mental consciousness and arises from the mind-faculty is called mental feeling (*citta-vedanā*).
Alternatively, it is said to be threefold, namely:
Regarding suffering, pleasure, and equanimity:
the experience that receives what is disagreeable and gives rise to affliction is called the sensation of suffering;
the experience that receives what is agreeable and gives rise to satisfaction is called the sensation of pleasure.
The neutral state of the objective sphere that abandons the extremes of suffering and pleasure is called the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
Alternatively, it is said to be fivefold, namely:
Regarding suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity:
if they occur within the five sensory consciousnesses of the desire realm, that which is oppressive is called suffering,
while that which is gratifying is termed pleasure.
In the stage of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), deliberation and distress are termed "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*);
pleasurable satisfaction is called "joy" (*saumanasya*).
In the stage of the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñānakāya*), a state of neutral reception is described as "equanimity" (*upekṣā*).
If one is in the first dhyāna, the mental satisfaction within the three groups of consciousness—those of the eye, ear, and body—is called pleasure (*sukha*);
the mental satisfaction is called joy (*prīti*).
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) pervades all four types of consciousness.
If one is in the second dhyāna, joy and equanimity are present in the mind,
and there is no other meaning.
If one is in the third dhyāna, bliss and equanimity are present in the mind.
There is no further meaning;
above the fourth dhyāna, there is only mental equanimity (upekṣā),
and no further meaning.
Alternatively, it is said to be sixfold,
referring to the feeling associated with the six consciousnesses.
Alternatively, it is divided into eighteen.
Within each of the first six, there are respectively suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure;
alternatively, these are further described as thirty-six feelings.
Within the first eighteen, each has both afflicted and purified aspects.
Or there may be one hundred and eight,
as Nāgārjuna has stated:
the first thirty-six are explained according to the distinctions of the three periods of time.
These are subdivided into immeasurable categories;
they are taught as the objects of mindfulness of feeling,
with their expansion and contraction being indefinite.
In total, there is only the single mind;
it may be divided into two, namely,
the outflowing (sāsrava) and the non-outflowing (anāsrava).

Furthermore, the categories of the determinate (*niyata*), the indeterminate (*aniyata*), the retribution (*vipāka*), and that which is neither retribution nor its cause (*avipāka-avipākahetu*) can also be divided into two;
or they may be said to be three:
the wholesome (*kuśala*), the unwholesome (*akuśala*), and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Furthermore, the trained (śaikṣa), the untrained (aśaikṣa), and that which is neither trained nor untrained (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa) can also be divided into three;
or they may be said to be four.
The contaminated (sāsrava) is likewise divided into three.
Wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate;
with the untainted as one,
they may also be said to be five.
The contaminated (sāsrava) are divided into three;
the uncontaminated (anāsrava) are divided into two:
those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Some describe it as six,
namely the six consciousnesses;
others divide it into nine.
The desire realm has three [types]:
wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
The form realm has two.
Wholesome and indeterminate;
the formless realm is likewise.
Together with the preceding, these constitute seven.
The untainted [factors] are divided into two:
those of training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Together with the preceding, there are nine.
Alternatively, it is said that there are twelve:
four in the desire realm,
namely, the wholesome, the unwholesome, the obscured-unspecified, and the unobscured-unspecified.
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are three [types of karma],
excluding the previously mentioned unwholesome (akuśala) ones.
It is the same for the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Including the preceding, there are ten;
the untainted (anāsrava) are divided into two:
the learner (śaikṣa) and the one beyond learning (aśaikṣa), which together with the preceding make twelve.
Some say there are twenty:
eight in the desire realm and one innate wholesome [state].
The wholesome [factors] associated with skillful means constitute two; the unwholesome constitute three;
and the obscured-unspecified constitutes the fourth.
The two types seen in proximity are called "concealed.
There are four kinds of non-concealed neutral states:
those born of retribution, those of deportment, those of craftsmanship, and those of transformation.
Including the preceding, there are eight.
In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are six,
excluding the previously mentioned unwholesome mind and the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika-citta*).
All others possess them.
In the formless realm, there are four;
excluding the deportment and transformation [minds] found within the form realm.
There are four other types.
However, all afflictions (*kleśa*) in the two higher realms are termed "concealed" (*nivṛta*),
which differs from those in the desire realm.
The preceding eighteen are with-outflow (sāsrava) minds.
The outflow-free (anāsrava) are divided into two:
those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Including the preceding twenty,
these are subdivided into immeasurable categories;
these are described as the objects of mental attention.
The objects of focus for the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) are necessarily only three:
first, conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma);
second, unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma).
Third is the dharma of principle.
Among conditioned phenomena, there are two types;
the first is mental phenomena.
These refer to perception, mental formations, and so forth;
secondly, there are non-material and non-mental factors,
namely the fourteen dissociated [formations] and others.
There are three unconditioned phenomena:
space, analytical cessation, and non-analytical cessation.
Their underlying principle refers to emptiness, signlessness, and so forth.
These are subdivided into immeasurable categories;
these are described as the objects of the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Such are their distinctions in characteristics.
Next, the distinctions in the abandonment of hindrances are discussed:
in the Abhidharma method, mindfulness alone is able to abandon them,
while the other two cannot.
This is because when mindfulness of multiple phenomena works together to support one another in the method of cultivation, it is able to effect abandonment;
whereas mindfulness of the individual nature (*svabhāva*) alone lacks power and therefore cannot effect abandonment.
Question:
In that school, there is no wisdom that exists alone;
why, then, is it necessary to proclaim that wisdom alone does not cease?
The commentary states:
Wisdom does not indeed function in isolation;
it is only for the purpose of refuting those who maintain that there are no mental factors (caitta).
Therefore, it is said that the nature of wisdom alone cannot sever [afflictions].
Because the mind is distracted and not concentrated,
its perception of objects is not clear.
Therefore it is not interrupted.
Furthermore, because the objects of thought and discourse are not actual mental formations,
it is therefore not interrupted.
Question: One observes that during the preceding seven stages of preparatory application (*saptaprayoga*), the mind does not uniformly sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
How, then, can [the practice of] the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) effect their severance?
The commentary states:

One sees that the continuous mindfulness of the common [characteristics] prior [to the path] does not have the capacity for severance; however, once the Path is attained, the mindfulness of the dharmas of common characteristics possesses the power of severance.
This is merely said in reference to that context.
Within the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra), it is not taught that there is the sense of "shared mindfulness" occurring simultaneously;
rather, it is held that wisdom alone performs the discernment.
The preceding and succeeding [factors] assist one another, and thus they may also be severed together.
In the Mahāyāna teachings, there is no fixed determination regarding the textual order;
rather, one should infer this based on the underlying meaning.
All three types are severed.
This is because the Bodhisattva’s mind abides in the true reality (*dharmatā*); as it awakens to and illuminates whatever arises, all obstructions are eliminated.
The coarse analysis of the three types of foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is thus concluded. These three gates are now finished.
Next, regarding the distinction between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
there are two types of foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
The first is the exclusive dharma (*kevaladharma*).
First, the "exclusive dharmas" (ekāṅga-dharma): all contemplative practices are subsumed into a single gateway of the four foundations of mindfulness; therefore, they are called exclusive dharmas.
Second, the "shared dharmas" (sādhāraṇa-dharma):
with respect to their commonality with other practices, they are collectively termed the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; therefore, they are called shared dharmas.

If one considers the four foundations of mindfulness within the context of the unique Dharma (asādhāraṇa-dharma), their cultivation is broad and encompasses both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
If one considers them within the common gate of the Hīnayāna teachings, the four foundations of mindfulness are tainted.
Those that are untainted (anāsrava) are categorized under other gates;
within the Mahāyāna Dharma, both tainted and untainted [dharmas] are included,
though for those at the stage of initial learning, they are tainted.
When perfected, it is untainted (*anāsrava*).
This is because, according to the Mahāyāna, the untainted exists prior to [the stage of] vision.
Therefore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
What are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment in the Mahāyāna?
A bodhisattva does not give rise to false conceptualizations regarding the body,
nor do they grasp at anything as being either non-existent or non-non-existent.
The remaining applications of mindfulness are likewise so.
These constitute the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment of the Mahāyāna;
therefore, one should know that they are untainted (*anāsrava*).
These two meanings are present within the stage of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
This applies to all other categories, whether they concern unique dharmas (*kevaladharma*) or shared dharmas (*sādhāraṇadharma*).
One should know that these four categories have now been concluded.
Next, we shall discuss the meaning of the sequence of the four foundations of mindfulness.
For what reason are they taught starting with the foundation of mindfulness of the body and ending with the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena?
There are two interpretations.
First, the sequence of coarse and subtle:
form is coarse and easy to observe;
therefore, it is explained first.
The sensation of subtle form is coarse compared to the latter two;
it is like when a person suffering from pain in their hands,
feet, or other limbs perceives it first with the mind.
Therefore, it is distinguished next.

Although the substance of the mind is subtler than perception (saṃjñā) and mental formations (saṃskāra), perception and formations, together with unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma), constitute the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
Thus, the mindfulness of phenomena is the most subtle.
The mind is coarser than that;
therefore, the mind is explained next,
followed by its phenomena.
Second is the sequential order of contemplation.
Since ordinary beings have traditionally given rise to afflictions through men regarding women’s forms and women regarding men’s forms,
one first contemplates the body.
Furthermore, form is the primary gateway among the sense bases;
therefore, one first contemplates the body.
Upon seeing the impurity of the body, one then forms this thought:
How is it that sentient beings delight in and cling to this form? It is because of craving for pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
Therefore, one next contemplates feeling (*vedanā*).
Furthermore, one further investigates: "Who is it that experiences this pleasure?"
This is what is called mind-consciousness;
therefore, one next contemplates the mind.
One further investigates: "Who is it that causes this mind to act?"
This refers to what is called "self.
Therefore, one subsequently contemplates phenomena (*dharma*).
Such is the sequence; thus concludes this fifth gate.
Next, the characteristics of contemplation are explained.
Once the practitioner has left the household life, they first maintain pure precepts;
then, within a state of tranquil concentration, they observe the impurity of internal and external forms.
To cultivate revulsion for one's own body, one contemplates the physical form of the body as five kinds of impurity.
The first is impurity of the seed:
this body takes past karma and afflictions as its seed.
First, the impurity of the seed: at present, the semen and blood of the parents serve as the seed;
this is called the impurity of the seed.
Second, the impurity of the dwelling place.
One places one's own body between the stomach and the large intestine within the mother’s womb.
Third, regarding the impurity of one's own body:
the body is a collection of thirty-six substances.
Fourth is impurity by its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇāśubhatā*).
The nine orifices constantly flow [with impurities].
These nine orifices are the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the mouth, and the passages for feces and urine.
From the eyes flow rheum and tears; from the ears, wax accumulates;
from the nostrils, mucus issues forth; from the mouth, saliva and vomit emerge;
and from the passages of excretion, feces and urine flow out.
Fifth, it is ultimately impure:
once this body has died, it is devoured by worms and becomes excrement;
when burned by fire, it turns to ash.
When buried, it turns into earth;
upon thorough investigation, not even the slightest mark of purity can be found.
Therefore, it is called ultimately impure.
If the mind becomes distracted, one should contemplate the impermanence of the body, the suffering of the three evil realms, and the imminent extinction of the Buddha-dharma;
by using these as a whip for the mind, one causes it to return and dwell securely within the contemplation of impurity.
To cultivate revulsion for the bodies of others, one must contemplate external forms through the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*).

These are: the notion of death, bloating, discoloration, festering, disintegration, being smeared with blood, being devoured by worms, the skeleton, and the separation of the limbs. This is the ninefold contemplation.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, one of the meditations on death is omitted;
by adding the meditation on burning, they are combined to form nine.
This meaning has been fully and extensively analyzed in the previous chapter on the Nine Meditations (Navasaṃjñā).
Mindfulness of the body is thus.
Although the body is impure, if there is even a slight matter of pleasure, it may still be considered pleasant;
therefore, one next contemplates feeling (*vedanā*).
One sees that there is only suffering.
What is the meaning of this?
There are three kinds of sensation.
These are what are called suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Within the sensation of suffering, there are three types of suffering:
namely, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
The two feelings of pleasure and equanimity each possess two types of suffering,
namely the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*),
as stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
This meaning is explained in detail as in the Chapter on the Four Noble Truths.
Although sensation is thus [impermanent], if there were even the slightest thing permanent within it, it would still be desirable;
therefore, one next contemplates the mind.
One observes that the characteristics of the mind arise and cease in a continuous flow,
like a whirling firebrand where each successive segment is distinct;
such is the nature of the mind.
There are three kinds of impermanence.
First is the impermanence of fragmentation,
wherein the minds of the six realms of existence differ from one another.
Second is the impermanence of thought,
which undergoes the flux of the four characteristics within a single kṣaṇa.
Third is the impermanence of the lack of substantial reality in intrinsic nature.
Conditioned phenomena are a hollow collection and possess not a single permanent nature.
This meaning has been fully analyzed in detail previously in the Udāna chapter.
Such is the reflection of the mind.
Although the mind is impermanent, if there were a self (ātman) that acts with sovereign power, such a matter might still be desirable;
therefore, one next contemplates phenomena (dharma) and perceives that they are merely selfless.
There are two kinds of selflessness:
first, the selflessness of sentient beings;
second, the selflessness of phenomena.
This meaning has been fully and extensively analyzed through these six gates in the preceding chapter on Non-Self.
Next, following the sūtra, the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is explained; therein, one first contemplates the internal body.
Next, one contemplates the external body;
subsequently, one contemplates both together.
What constitutes the "internal," and why then speak of the "external"?
If analyzed according to the twelve bases (*āyatana*),
the six sense organs of all sentient beings constitute the internal,
while the six objects constitute the external.
Now, among the four foundations of mindfulness, one's own body is called "internal" and another's body is called "external.
Why are they distinguished individually at first and then treated collectively afterward?
The term "relinquishing" (*śīla*) has two meanings.
First, the afflictions to be abandoned differ:
some people are attached primarily to internal states while their attachment to external states is slight.
Just as a person might abandon their parents, wife, children, and wealth for the sake of their own body,
so too must one be taught to contemplate the internal because of an excessive attachment to the internal.
Alternatively, there may be someone who has a greater attachment to external things and a lesser attachment to internal things.
Just as a person might lose their body and forfeit their life for the sake of wealth,
because one is attached to external objects to such an extent, one must be taught to contemplate the external.
Since some people are attached to both [the internal and the external], they must practice combined contemplation.
Second is the contemplation of following.
One who practices in successive order originally perceives signs of purity within their own body.
Therefore, one first observes the internal;
when it is not found within, one supposes it exists externally,
and thus observes the external once again.
When observing the internal first, one does not reach the external;
when observing the external, one likewise does not reach the internal.
Therefore, in the third stage, one observes the internal and external in combination.
Regarding the contemplation of the internal,
the scriptural text states:
"One contemplates the internal body by way of following the body in contemplation."
With diligence and single-mindedness, one eliminates worldly greed and anxiety.
"Contemplating the internal body" refers to the specific objects of observation;
"contemplating the body in accordance with its nature" reveals the characteristics of that contemplation.
"Following" (*anuvicca*) means "in accordance with.
Thoroughly and completely observing the characteristics of the body is called the "contemplation of the body" (*kāyānupaśyanā*).
One should apply oneself with diligence and single-mindedness to clarify the ritual of this contemplation.
The practitioner now wishes to destroy the characteristics of the body;
this cannot be accomplished without diligent effort,
and therefore one must be ardent and persevering.
Therefore, Nāgārjuna said:
"It is easy to part from ordinary people;
it is difficult to part from those one knows."
It is easy to part from acquaintances;
it is difficult to part from relatives.
It is easy to part from relatives.
It is difficult to separate from one's own body;
therefore, a practitioner who now wishes to separate from their own body must be diligent.
Diligence arises from single-mindedness; thus, it is called "one-pointedness of mind."
The phrase "removing worldly greed and sorrow" clarifies that which is free from various defilements.
Why, then, is it specifically said to "remove worldly greed and sorrow"?
Nāgārjuna explains:
In this state, the practitioner frequently gives rise to greed and anxiety;
therefore, their removal is specifically taught.
How does one frequently give rise [to these] at the very moment of first abandoning the five desires?
Because one recollects what was formerly loved, greed arises frequently;
because one has not yet attained the Dharma of the Path, sorrow arises frequently.
Therefore, it is specifically said that one eliminates worldly greed and sorrow.
Furthermore, when ordinary beings give rise to craving, it is difficult to abandon;
its power to bring about rebirth is strong, and it is the foremost of the three poisons.
Therefore, among all afflictions, craving is specifically taught as that which must be eliminated.
The faculty of sorrow arises solely from sensual desire;
it is the heaviest obstacle to meditative concentration and is thus abandoned first within the dhyānas.
Therefore, among the five feelings, it is specifically said that sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is eliminated;
if greed is said to be eliminated, the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*) vanish accordingly,
and if sorrow is said to be eliminated, the remaining feelings are likewise dispelled.
It is like splitting bamboo: the first joint is the most difficult;
once the first joint is split, all the remaining joints fall away in succession.
So it is with greed and sorrow.
The following clarifies the contemplation of the external and the contemplation of both the internal and external;
the same applies by analogy.
Within the mindfulness of sensation (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*) as well, one first contemplates the internal, then the external, and finally both together.
Among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), feeling (*vedanā*) is exclusively an external phenomenon because it is subsumed under the [mental] base. However,
within the present context of the four foundations of mindfulness, one's own feeling is internal and another's feeling is external.
Furthermore, that which is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is internal;
that which is associated with the five [sensory] consciousnesses is termed external.
Moreover, that which is definitely experienced (*niyatavedanīya*) may also be described as internal.
Scattered sensations are categorized as external.
Regarding these internal and external [sensations], there is first a distinction and subsequently a synthesis.
Within the context of mental attention as well, one first contemplates the internal, then the external, and finally both together.
Among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the mind is comprised solely within the internal sense faculty of the mind (*manas*).
Now, within the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one's own mind is considered internal,
while the minds of others are considered external.
Furthermore, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is termed internal,
while the five [sensory] consciousnesses are termed external;
likewise, a concentrated mind may also be described as internal.
The distracted mind is considered "external.
Within the practice of mindfulness of dharmas, one first contemplates the internal,
then the external, and finally both together.
The internal refers to mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
The external refers to that which is neither form nor mind—the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
Among these, the observation of their characteristics is entirely the same as in the first gate.
Next, the four right efforts (catur-samyak-prahāṇa) are analyzed through five gates.
First, the explanation of their names.
First, the essential nature of the two concentrations;
second, the differentiation of their modes of activity;
third, the discussion of their sequence.
Fifth, the detailed analysis of their characteristics.
What are their names? Regarding the term "right effort" (*samyak-prahāṇa*):
To practice with diligence and without indolence is called "exertion" (*vīrya*). When the mind of exertion is not deviant, it is called "rectitude."
This is stated to be correct.
[The opponent] asks:
For what reason are the foundations of mindfulness, the faculties, the powers, and so forth [taught]?
While none of them speak of this as being correct, Nāgārjuna alone discusses it in his commentary,
explaining that when diligence is stirred up, joy enters into what is erroneous.
In order to prevent those faults, one specifically discusses right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*),
because this right effort is characterized by great activity,
unlike that of the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Most [practitioners] exert themselves with diligence yet follow what is perverse and inverted;
conversely, to be free from those faults is declared to be "correct. This concludes this section.
Next, the essential nature is determined.
These four right endeavors all take diligence as their mental factor for their essence.
Although their essence is one,
they are divided into four according to their respective functions.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"Just as a single moment of a lamp possesses four capacities—
it can both burn the wick and exhaust the oil."
It can both heat the vessel and dispel darkness;
right effort is likewise,
for it possesses these four capacities and is therefore divided into four types.
Question: That lamp possesses four capacities in a single moment,
but diligent effort does not.
The preceding and following sections are divided into four parts.
How is it that they resemble a simile?
To explain:
The methods for establishing analogies are not of a single kind;
they may take a partial aspect, a majority of aspects, or even the whole.
The analogy established here takes a partial aspect and not the whole.
They cannot be held equally accountable.
Furthermore, within the state of diligence (*vīrya*), there is also the sense that a single moment of thought possesses the four capacities.
For example, at the time when a single moment of the Path (*mārga*) manifests:
To cause already arisen afflictions to fail in their function as causes is called "abandoning what has already arisen.
To obstruct future afflictions so that their fruits do not arise is called "abandoning what has not yet arisen.
This very path has never previously arisen.
The initial cultivation and arising is called "cultivating what has not yet arisen.
Augmenting prior wholesome states to cause them to increase and expand is called "cultivating what has already arisen.
Based on this meaning, it is said to be like a lamp.
Question: Is "diligence" (āyoga) restricted solely to the wholesome,
or does it also apply to other meanings?
The commentators differ on this point.
In the Abhidharma system, diligence (*vīrya*) exists only in the wholesome,
because it is enumerated among the universal wholesome mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, diligence is explained as penetrating all three natures; however,
in the present treatise, we discuss virtuous diligence (*kuśala-vīrya*),
which is correctly identified by distinguishing it from the other two.
Question: The *Smṛtyupasthāna-śāstra* states that there are three types:
by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), by association (*samprayoga*), and by object (*ālambana*).
What is right effort?
It is explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* that there are two kinds of right effort.
There are both intrinsic and concomitant [types].
Regarding the intrinsic, the treatise itself explains:
"For the sake of seeking the Path, one gives rise to four kinds of diligence within the mental factors."
This is called its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding the shared [nature], the treatise states:
"The path arises with diligence as its primary causal condition."
Whether they be outflowing or non-outflowing, whether material or non-material—all such things are entirely comprised within right effort; this is called "shared.
Furthermore, there must also be an object-condition.
The text is abbreviated and does not state it explicitly;
the conduct that is exerted constitutes the condition (*pratyaya*).
These two sections are concluded.
Next is the analysis of conduct (*caryā-vibhaṅga*).
The categories of diligence (*vīrya*) universally encompass all forms of conduct;
however, because they follow various divergent theories regarding conduct, their specific classifications are difficult to calculate.
Now, based on one gate, these are provisionally divided into four.
Of these four, the first two clarify the diligent abandonment of evil,
while the latter two clarify the cultivation of goodness.
Cessation of evil and practice of the good:
this is the sequence of the Dharma.
Evil exists in the past and the future;
goodness exists in the past and the future.
Therefore, they are divided into four kinds.
Question: Since that which has already arisen as evil has already ceased and passed away, and that which is present lacks intrinsic nature,
what is there to be abandoned?
There are three meanings of "understanding" (or "resolution"):
first, although an evil that has already arisen has passed into the past, at the time it originally arose, it possessed the sense of being a cause for the production of what follows;
by presently practicing the antidote, one severs its sense of being a cause for the production of what follows.
This is called "having abandoned what has already arisen.
Second, although unwholesome states that have already arisen have passed into the past, they are still acquired by means of an acquisition (*prāpti*) residing at the limit of the present mind.
By abandoning their present acquisition, one ensures that those past evils do not come to belong to oneself again.
This is called "the abandonment of what has already arisen.
Third, although previously arisen evils have ceased, their lineage continues to arise;
by presently cultivating the antidote, one cuts off that lineage—this is called "the abandonment of what has already arisen."
Question: If one who has severed the category of that which has already arisen is called "one who has severed what has arisen," then since the category exists in the future,
why is one not called "one who has severed what has not yet arisen"?
The commentary states:
When one minutely investigates, that which is of a nature capable of being abandoned is actually yet to arise;
however, because this refers specifically to those of a nature already arisen—as distinguished from those that have not yet arisen at all—it is said that what has already arisen is abandoned.
Question: Once it has been well initiated and completed,
how is it to be cultivated?
The term "already arisen" (*utpanna*) has three meanings.

First, when a wholesome state that has already arisen is about to originate from its cause, it possesses the sense of being the cause for the subsequent arising [of further wholesome states]. Second, by practicing wholesome dharmas in the present, one establishes the sense that past wholesome states serve as causes;

thus, it is called "cultivating what has already arisen. Third, [it refers to] the fact that once a wholesome state has arisen, it persists through the power of its own nature. Therefore, it is termed "already arisen."

Second, the acquisition of manifestation (*samudācāra-prāpti*) that acquires past wholesome states and prevents them from being lost or destroyed is called "cultivation of what has already arisen" (*bhāvita-pūrva*).
This is like how, within the fifteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), there is the arising of an acquisition that acquires the wholesome states preceding them.
In this way, although all these previously arisen wholesome states have already reached completion, their specific types continue in succession.

To exert oneself in the cultivation of those types that have not yet arisen, so as to cause them to arise and thereby augment the previously arisen wholesome states, is called "cultivating what has already arisen."
Question:
Those types have not actually arisen;
for what reason is it said that they have been cultivated and produced?
This is explained in the same manner as before.
To distinguish these from those that have never arisen at all, the term "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) is added to the preceding term "wholesome" (*kuśala*) once these three gates have been completed.
Next, the sequence of their arising will be discussed.
Regarding the previous section on the abandonment of unwholesome states, why is it that in some instances the abandonment of unwholesome states already arisen is mentioned first,
while in others the abandonment of unwholesome states not yet arisen is mentioned first?
What is the meaning of this?
There are five kinds of understanding.
First, regarding the sequence of the arising of afflictions, one distinguishes by first severing those already arisen,
because those already arisen are coarse, and subsequently severing those not yet arisen.
Because they have not yet arisen, they are subtle; thus, like the obstacles of the first stage (*bhūmi*), which are coarse and arise first, these are severed first.
The obstacles of the second stage are subtle and arise later.
Therefore, they are excluded later.
In this manner, all [factors] are analyzed by contrasting them with the ignorance associated with the second and fourth stages of abiding.
Ignorance that has already arisen is termed "already produced";
the afflictions of the four abodes that arise subsequent to conditions are termed "not yet produced.
According to this principle, one first cuts off what is not yet produced and subsequently eliminates what is already produced.
The four abidings (*catvāraḥ sthitayaḥ*) that have not yet arisen are coarse and easily dispelled;
therefore, they are severed first.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) that has already arisen is subtle and difficult to separate from.
Therefore, they are excluded later.
Third, regarding the formation of arising through afflictions:
all afflictions possess the nature of arising.

Past afflictions that have arisen and passed away perfume the fundamental consciousness within the stage of ignorance (*avidyā-bhūmi*), where they accumulate to form seeds; this is termed "attainment" (*samanvāgama*).
The subsequent continuous arising of the same type of preceding afflictions is termed "manifestation" (*samudācāra*).
That which is currently arising is called "unborn" in relation to what preceded it.
If this meaning is accepted, one could also say that what was previously unborn is first abandoned, and what has already arisen is subsequently eliminated.
What is the meaning of this?

When the Path arises, one first cultivates skillful means to suppress what is currently manifesting, so that what has not yet arisen does not come into operation; this is called "severing the unarisen.
Subsequently, one severs the seeds originally established; this is called "severing the already-arisen."
Fourth, regarding the distinction between afflictions and their acquisition:
within this framework, it is also taught that one first abandons what has not yet arisen and subsequently abandons what has already arisen.
What is the meaning of this?
When the Noble Path first arises, it first severs the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the afflictions associated with the mind;
by preventing them from continuing in the future, this is called "severing what has not yet arisen.
Because their acquisition has been severed, past afflictions are prevented from coming back to belong to oneself.
This is called "having already abandoned.
Fifth, there is the classification according to the cause and fruit of the afflictions (*kleśa*):
past afflictions that have arisen previously are termed the "cause."
Prior to the arising of future afflictions, they are designated as "fruits.
In this context, the cause is termed "already arisen" and the fruit is termed "not yet arisen";
thus, within this framework, the already-arisen and the not-yet-arisen are severed at one and the same time.
What is the meaning of this?
The cause of delusion is the past; the fruit of delusion is the future.
The arising of the Path occurs in between, severing the connection between cause and fruit.
The non-attainment of the status of cause is called the severance of what has already arisen;
the non-attainment of the status of fruit is called the severance of what has not yet arisen.
Because a single path possesses both capacities, it is said to occur simultaneously.
The first two cases are as described above.

Regarding the latter two types, there is no further dispute concerning the fact that the former arises first for what has not yet arisen, while the latter increases what has already arisen. Why is this so?

To clarify that wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) which previously did not exist now come into being through the application of skillful cultivation: because they were previously non-existent, one first cultivates those not yet arisen;
once those not yet arisen have been produced, one further cultivates subsequent wholesomeness to augment and support the preceding wholesomeness—this is called "cultivating what has already arisen."
If one speaks from the perspective of those who have long cultivated within the wholesome, there is also the sense that what has already arisen was previously cultivated.
What is the meaning of this?
Practice consists of two parts.
The first is to review what is old; the second is to know what is new.
Between these two, one must first review what is old before knowing what is new.
This reviewing of what is old is called the cultivation of that which has already arisen.
That which knows the new is called the cultivation of what has not yet arisen.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of excellence:
first, that of one's own level (svabhāga), and second, that of further progress (viśeṣa).
One knows that what has already arisen is cultivated first to bring it to maturity,
while what has not yet arisen is cultivated later for its superior progress and entry. Therefore,
it is understood.
Within the category of the wholesome, there is also the sense of having previously cultivated that which has already arisen. These four gateways are concluded.
Next, the characteristics will be extensively analyzed.
Within the abandonment of unwholesome conduct, there are three distinctions.
First, the practice of repentance,
which consists solely of repenting for what has already arisen.
Second, the practice of guarding against faults.
The first [type of restraint] prevents only that which has not yet arisen;
the three types of abandonment of faulty conduct abandon both what has already arisen and what has not yet arisen.
What is the meaning of this?
To give rise to a mental state of remorse for evil already committed is called the practice of repentance (*kaukṛtya*).
Within this, there are three distinct types.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
"To repent and eliminate past transgressions in accordance with the Dharma is called non-negligence regarding the past."
That which has been transgressed in the present is to be repented according to the Dharma;
this is called heedful practice in the present.
That which will be transgressed in the future shall likewise be repented according to the Dharma.
This is called future heedfulness.
This involves generating a mind of remorse regarding evil that has already arisen throughout the three periods of time,
rather than regretting what has not yet arisen.
Although regret has already arisen, one can cause it not to continue after that point;
by further subdividing according to its meaning, one also prevents what has not yet arisen.
Such is the manner of repentance.

Regarding the prevention of faults (*āpatti-pratigha-saṃvara*), one carefully guards the mind against unarisen evils so that they do not manifest; this is called the practice of preventing transgressions.
Within this, there are two types of discernment, as explained in the *Bhūmivastu* (The Stage of Support).
First, by presently practicing the antidote so that past faults do not arise,
it is called having already performed the practice of heedfulness.
Second, one should cultivate the antidote so that future faults do not occur.
It is called "the practice of heedfulness," which guards against faults in this manner.
It is called "the practice of severing faults" because it causes the causes and effects of delusion to be severed so that they do not continue in succession.
Furthermore, severing all afflictions so that they no longer belong to oneself is also called "severing faults.
Within this, there are three stages of discernment,
and there is one type of practice.
Why is it said that one severs only the delusions of the present and not those of the past or future?
This means that one severs the ignorance of self-nature (svabhāva-avidyā) which is coessential with them.
Because the wisdom that contemplates conditions perceives phenomena as being solely true and devoid of deluded thoughts,
it can cause the innate ignorance of the same essence not to further project subsequent states;
this is termed "severance."
There is no further meaning beyond this.
Even if there were other meanings, they would not constitute a treatment based on identity;
therefore, they are now set aside and not discussed.
There is a type of practice that severs only what is past and future, but does not apply to the present.
What is the meaning of this?
That is to say:
having severed the coarse arising of afflictions characterized by distinct marks,
the delusions that arose in the past are designated as the cause.
