That which is to arise is the fruit;
the Path arises in between, severing cause and fruit.
To sever its past causes is called "cutting off the past."
The pacification of subsequent results is called "severing the future.
Because there is no delusion at the limit of the path,
one does not sever the present.
There is a certain practice that universally severs all faults of the three periods of time.
What is the meaning of this?
Past [dharmas] possess the fruit of delusion;
present [dharmas] possess the acquisition (prāpti) of delusion,
which maintains continuity and belongs to the person.
To presently cultivate the antidote, sever those afflictions, and ensure they do not drag one into future [existence] is called "severing the present.
To cause the causes and effects of the afflictions not to come and belong to oneself is called "severing the past and future."
Thus one is free from evil.
Within the gateway of cultivating goodness, there is a twofold distinction:
first, the distinction according to the mind.
Second, regarding the classification by way of cultivation,
there are three kinds of mind:
first, the mind of sympathetic joy.
The first is the mind of rejoicing, which concerns that which has already arisen.
The second is the mind of seeking,
which concerns that which has not yet arisen.
Third is the mind of dedication,
which universally dedicates all wholesome dharmas— both those already performed and those yet to be done— toward their intended goal.
Question: If joy (*prīti*) consists solely of rejoicing in what has already arisen, why does it say in the sūtras that one should give rise to joy by recollecting what is yet to be attained?
That [recollecting the future] could indeed be joy.
It is not called "rejoicing.
For the mind of rejoicing to be genuine, it must celebrate what has already arisen;
such is the nature of the mind.
Regarding the concise explanation of cultivation, there are two kinds.
The first is rehearsing what is familiar,
which consists solely of rehearsing that which has already arisen.
Second is knowing the new:
it only increases that which has not yet arisen.
Furthermore, there are two kinds.
The first is that which pertains to oneself,
having already been cultivated;
the second is superior progress.
Regarding the cultivation of that which has not yet arisen,
there are further two types:
first, the cultivation of acquisition (pratilambha-bhāvanā).
One attains that which has already arisen;
the categories of wholesome states that have already arisen,
whether they belong to the past or the future.
There is that which is called "the acquisition of acquisition" (*prāpti-prāpti*), which arises once [the primary acquisition] has already arisen.
Because it arises after [the primary acquisition], within those fifteen moments of mind during the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), it only further acquires what precedes it;
it does not acquire what follows.
Second is the cultivation of practice (*āsevana-bhāvanā*).
This refers to practicing solely that which has not yet arisen, so as to cultivate it until it arises.
Thus are the four types of diligence.
Next, the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) is analyzed through two gates.
First, a general explanation of its name.
Second, the definition of its essential nature and characteristics. As for its name,
the sūtras sometimes refer to it as the "bases of supernormal power" (ṛddhipāda).
Alternatively, it is also described as the "factor of wish-fulfillment" (pranidhānāṅga).
As for the "bases of psychic power" (ṛddhipāda), because one seeks meditative concentration through the four factors— desire and so forth— in accordance with one's wishes,
they are called "wish-fulfilling."
Mastery over the meditative attainments is like feet; thus they are called the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*).
As for the term "factors" (*aṅga*), it has the meaning of "cause";
that is, desire and the others are the causes of meditative concentration.
Since this concentration is designated by the name "member of the wish-fulfilling" (praṇidhānāṅga) based on its cause,
such is its name. What, then,
are its essential nature and characteristics?
These four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) have meditative concentration as their primary factor.
Because concentration varies according to its specific causes,
they are divided into four types.
This begins from the concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi*) up to the concentration of wisdom (*prajñā-samādhi*).
Regarding the "concentration of desire," the longing for higher tranquility is termed "desire."
Because one seeks to attain concentration through desire,
it is called "concentration through desire.
This is also acceptable.
The concentrated mind is obtained through desire;
because the fruit is designated according to its cause, it is called "desire-concentration" (*chanda-samādhi*).
As for "diligence-concentration" (*vīrya-samādhi*):
Diligently detesting lower faults and diligently seeking higher tranquility is called *vīrya* (diligence).
It is also appropriate to call it the "concentration of diligence" (*vīrya-samādhi*), as concentration is attained from diligence;
the concentrated mind is obtained through diligence.
It is called the concentration of diligence (*vīrya-samādhi*). As for what is termed "mindfulness concentration" (*smṛti-samādhi*),
in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* it is called "mental concentration" (*citta-samādhi*).
To maintain the mind and cause it to abide within the object of meditative concentration is called mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Mindfulness is able to attain concentration (*samādhi*).
Therefore, it is said that concentration arises from mindfulness;
this is also correct,
for the concentrated mind is attained through mindfulness.
It is called mindfulness-concentration (smṛti-samādhi).
Because it maintains the mind and abides upon its object,
it is further named mindfulness (smṛti).
Regarding what is called "wisdom-concentration" (prajñā-samādhi),
it is termed "contemplative concentration" (cintā-samādhi) in the *Bhūmi-sūtra*.
It consists of observing the faults of the lower stages and knowing the superior benefits of the higher ones.
It is called "wisdom" (prajñā); when one attains concentration through wisdom, it is termed "wisdom-concentration" (prajñā-samādhi).
This is also acceptable, for the concentrated mind is attained by means of wisdom.
Therefore, it is called the concentration of wisdom (*prajñā-samādhi*).
Yet, because this mind of wisdom reflects upon, discriminates, and seeks superior tranquility,
it is also called the concentration of reflection (*cintā-samādhi*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that one must cultivate five factors to seek the first dhyāna:
desire, thought, diligence, skillful wisdom, and single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*).
Now, within this [discourse on] the *ṛddhipāda*, single-mindedness is omitted.
It is because of their concealment and manifestation. Question:
The foundations of mindfulness possess three types.
Regarding the intrinsic nature and common conditions,
as in what manner?
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are two kinds.
There are both intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and commonality.
Regarding "intrinsic nature," there are two ways of understanding it.
First, its nature is established in terms of the specific modes of practice (*caryā*) that arise within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The fixed number is primary;
the fixed [categories] are distinguished by their causes;
therefore, desire and so forth are mentioned.
Second, its nature is distinguished according to the cause of concentration.
As Nāgārjuna says:
"The mind of desire is the primary factor."
By following this, one attains concentration;
even contemplating it as the primary focus,
one attains concentration by following it.
This is called the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding the "shared" [nature], the treatise states:
it is the path produced by the causes and conditions of the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*).
If both outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) wholesome aggregates (*kuśalaskandha*) arise together, they are all termed "at will" (*yatheṣṭa*).
This is called "conjoined.
By analogy with what precedes, there should also be "conditioned-at-will" (*ālambana-yatheṣṭa*).
The text is abbreviated and does not explain it.
Next, the five faculties (pañcendriya) are explained through a fourfold analysis.
First, explaining its name;
second, discerning its characteristics;
third, discussing its sequence.
Fourth, the classification according to stages:
what are their names?
They are the faculty of faith, up to and including the faculty of wisdom.
Certainty regarding the object is called faith (*śraddhā*);
refining the mind toward the Dharma is called diligence (*vīrya*);
and the focused application of that diligent mind toward its goal is described as progress (*pragraha*).
Guarding the objective sphere is called mindfulness;
abiding upon the object is called concentration;
and penetrating through observation is called wisdom.
These five kinds of past habitual tendencies have now been established;
that which is capable of producing [a result] is called a "root" (*indriya*).
Such is the name for this section, which concludes this first gate.
Next, its characteristics are distinguished.
Within the faculty of faith, the manner of opening and closing is indeterminate;
in total, it is but a single kind.
Alternatively, it is divided into two:
faith in the cause and faith in the result,
as explained in the *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra*.
To have faith in the bodhisattva practices is the cause of faith.
To have faith in all the Buddha-dharmas...
This is the fruit of faith.
As it is with the Mahāyāna,
so it is with the Hīnayāna.
Alternatively, it is divided into three, namely:
faith in the Three Jewels.
Alternatively, they are divided into four,
as stated in the *Tattvasiddhi*:
the four unshakable faiths (*avetyaprasāda*).
Faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, and the precepts—
these are its four [refuges].
Alternatively, they may be divided into five.
That is to say:
having faith in the Three Jewels;
having faith in causes and faith in results.
Alternatively, it is divided into six:
faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha;
faith in causes; faith in results; and faith in the ultimate truth.
Alternatively, it is divided into eight,
as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and the supernormal powers of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
These constitute four;
adding the conviction in various causes and the conviction in various results,
they total five.
Faith in the true meaning;
together with the preceding [faiths], these constitute six.
These include faith in the attainment of that meaning and faith in the attainment of the means.
Including the preceding [categories], there are eight.
Unsurpassed Bodhi is the meaning of "attainment.
The Bodhisattva’s training in the Path is the means for attainment.
If expanded, they are immeasurable;
within the faculty of diligence, the meanings are likewise not fixed,
yet in total, there is only one.
Alternatively, it is divided into two:
namely, physical and mental;
these are the two kinds of diligence.
Alternatively, it is explained as threefold,
as stated in the *Bhūmivastu*:
first, the diligence of the great vow.
Second, the gathering of wholesome dharmas;
third, benefiting sentient beings,
as explained at length therein.
Some speak of four kinds,
as in the case of the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Others speak of five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten.
And as with the *Dharmasaṃgraha*,
the meaning within the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) is likewise not fixed;
in sum, it is only one.
Alternatively, it is divided into two:
first, hearing and retaining,
which refers to upholding the teachings of the Dharma.
Second is the retention of meaning (*arthadhāraṇī*),
which is able to retain the teachings regarding their meanings;
alternatively, it may be divided into three types.
That is to say:
it refers to recollecting the true merits of the Three Jewels;
alternatively, it may be divided into four [aspects].
One contemplates the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and one contemplates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Alternatively, these may be divided into six, namely:
The six recollections consist of mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, the precepts, generosity, and the devas; these are the six.
Alternatively, they may be divided into eight.
As Nāgārjuna stated:
"Beyond the previous six, two additional types are added:
mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation, and mindfulness of death."
This is the eighth [set].
Alternatively, they may be divided into ten,
as Nāgārjuna has explained.
To the preceding eight types, one further adds mindfulness of the body and mindfulness of cessation;
these constitute the ten.
Mindfulness that seeks the joy of supramundane quiescence is called mindfulness of cessation.
Alternatively, they are divided into eleven,
as stated in the *Dharmaskandha-sūtra*:
mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and mindfulness of the Bodhisattvas.
He recollects the bodhisattva practices and the perfections;
he recollects the ten stages and the indestructible powers;
he recollects the fearlessnesses and the unique qualities.
Up to not being separated from mindfulness of all-knowledge—
this is the eleventh.
The first four types consist of being mindful of what one has studied.
Next, there are three kinds that consist of reflecting upon what has been practiced;
following these, there are four kinds that consist of reflecting upon what has been accomplished.
If explained in detail, they are immeasurable.
The meaning within the faculty of concentration is likewise not fixed;
in brief, it is one,
or it may be divided into two.
There are mundane and supramundane [attainments].
Worldly pure concentration is termed mundane.
The untainted supramundane can likewise be divided into three types.
First, with vitarka and vicāra,
namely the first dhyāna and so forth;
second, without vitarka but with vicāra.
This refers to the intermediate dhyāna;
it is without vitarka and without vicāra.
This refers to all samādhis from the second dhyāna upward.
Alternatively, they are divided into four types:
namely, regression, abiding, progress, and certainty;
these four are as fully and extensively analyzed in the previous chapter on the eight dhyānas.
Some say there are five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten,
as explained in the "Dhyāna Chapter" of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*.
If expanded, they are immeasurable.
The meaning within the faculty of wisdom is likewise not fixed;
in general, it is one,
or it may be divided into two.
First, the condition of worldly truth;
second, the condition of ultimate truth.
Furthermore, there are those that are with outflows and without outflows, mundane and supramundane, and so forth.
All can be divided into two;
they can also be divided into three.
That is to say:
Hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Furthermore, it is taught within the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* that *prajñā-vipaśyanā* and *jñāna* likewise constitute three types.
Prajñā is wisdom;
vipaśyanā is contemplation;
jñāna is knowledge.
Prajñā (wisdom) cognizes the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) through specific characteristics;
vipaśyanā (insight) cognizes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) through general characteristics;
and jñāna (gnosis) destroys characteristics, transcends existence and non-existence, and cognizes the single true essence.
There are many gateways to these three;
I have merely cited these as examples.
Alternatively, they are explained as being fourfold.
Hearing, reflection, cultivation, and realization;
or they are said to be five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten,
as in the *Bhūmivastu* (Dichilun).
The subdivisions are immeasurable.
Such are the essential characteristics; this concludes the two preceding sections.
Next, the sequence will be discussed.
The five realities exist simultaneously;
however, for the sake of this discussion, we shall treat them in sequence according to the characteristics of their cultivation.
Faith is the foremost of practices.
Therefore, one first clearly understands through faith;
because one practices based on faith, diligence follows next;
and by means of diligence, one does not forget the Dharma.
Therefore, mindfulness is explained next;
because of the presence of mindfulness, one abides in the Dharma without wavering.
Hence, concentration is explained next.
Because the mind is tranquil, wisdom attains illumination;
therefore, wisdom is explained last.
The sequence is thus.
Among these five faculties, wisdom is the primary leader,
while the other four are its attendants. Question:
Among the factors of the path, wisdom is primary.
Since the foundations of mindfulness are wisdom,
they are listed first.
Among the five faculties, wisdom serves as the primary one.
Why is it not listed first, but rather placed later?
The explanation states:
There are two sequences for discerning dharmas:
first, the sequence of exposition,
in which the primary element is mentioned first and its associates follow.
Second, the sequence of cultivation:
from inferior to superior.
Within the section on the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are listed first.
This explains the sequential order.
Now, among the five faculties, the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya) is mentioned last;
this is the order of cultivation.
Furthermore, wisdom possesses many capacities;
first, it is able to initiate [the path].
Therefore, among the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa), the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are explained first.
Second, they are able to lead to the end;
therefore, among the five faculties, they are listed last. There is yet another distinct meaning [to this].
These two points will be fully analyzed and explained later.
Next, regarding the classification by stages:
in reality, these five factors pervade the entire course from beginning to end;
however, they are provisionally divided according to their characteristics as explained in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*.
The stage of initial practice (*ādikarmika-bhūmi*) is termed the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
The stage prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is called the stage of initial practice because one is able to have faith and accord with the supramundane path.
The faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*) is present in the stage of "seeing the truths" (*darśanamārga*),
because practice proceeds with speed therein.
The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) is present in the stage of "thinning out" (*tanūbhūmi*).
Because the Sakṛdāgāmin maintains the mind by abiding in its object and because their afflictions are attenuated,
it is called the faculty of concentration (samādhīndriya) when they dwell in the stage of freedom from desire.
Because the Anāgāmin has attained the eight dhyānas...
In the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), it is called the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya).
Because the Arhat has attained the ultimate goal,
the meaning is the same when one uses a lesser term to represent a greater one.
The five faculties are thus.
The five powers are like the faculties.
Next, the seven factors of enlightenment are explained.
The analysis consists of four sections:
first, the explanation of its name;
second, the determination of its essential nature and components.
Regarding the three divisions of śamatha and vipaśyanā,
what are the names of the four clarifications of their sequence?
In the sūtras, these are described as the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), also called the limbs of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
Untainted noble wisdom (*anāsrava-āryaprajñā*) is termed "enlightenment" (*bodhi*);
the seven types, such as mindfulness and so forth, are distinguished as its "factors" (*aṅga*) or "limbs" (*pakṣa*).
Furthermore, the noble wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) may be called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*).
The seven factors, such as mindfulness (*smṛti*), which can serve as its causes, are termed "limbs" (*aṅga*) or "factors" (*bhāga*).
Question: [What is the meaning of this?]
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are all equally factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*) and branches of awakening (*bodhyanga*).
Why, then, are these seven specifically designated as "branches of awakening"?
Because the seven factors of awakening are proximate to the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).
Because these proximate fruits manifest the characteristics of their causes, they are specifically designated as "limbs" (*aṅga*) and "parts" (*bhāga*) in relation to awakening.
Such is the meaning of the terms; this concludes the first section.
Next is the determination of the essential nature,
which is analyzed according to three meanings.
First is the analysis in relation to the fruit.
The fruit is designated as "awakening" (bodhi);
these seven factors are merely limbs of awakening (bodhyaṅga) and are not themselves called awakening.
Because they act as causes for the fruit,
they are called factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*);
because they are not the essence of the fruit itself, they are not called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*).
Second, regarding the analysis based on the correlation with the seven factors:
the single factor of *dharmapravicaya* (investigation of phenomena) is an awakening (*bodhi*) but not a limb (*aṅga*).
Its essence is wisdom (*prajñā*).
Therefore, it is given the name "awakening" (*bodhi*).
Because it is not a cause for wisdom (*prajñā*), it is not called a factor of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*).
The other six are factors, yet they are not called awakening.
Because it acts as the cause for the arising of awakening,
it is called a "limb" (aṅga); it is not,
however, the essence of wisdom itself.
Therefore, it is not termed "awakening.
Third, there is a classification according to the stages of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*).
These seven types constitute the general stage of cultivation.
Each is designated as a "limb" (aṅga) because they collectively serve as the general cause.
Within this context, the single factor of the investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya) is both awakening (bodhi) and a limb of awakening (bodhyaṅga).
Because its essence is wisdom (prajñā), it is termed "awakening."
They are called factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) because they constitute the stage of complete cultivation;
the others are not so called because they are not wisdom.
Since they constitute the stage of complete cultivation, they may be designated as "factors" (*aṅga*).
The analysis presented in this treatise concludes with these two gates.
Next, śamatha and vipaśyanā are distinguished:
meditative concentration (samādhi) and awakening (bodhi) constitute śamatha.
Tranquility and equanimity assist and accomplish it;
the discernment of phenomena is insight;
diligence and joy—these two factors assist and accomplish it.
When mindfulness is present, both are simultaneously harmonized.
It is asked:
Within the Eightfold Noble Path, diligence serves as the universal guide.
Why is it that mindfulness and equanimity are both harmonized therein?
The explanation is:
they mutually accord with principle, and thus should be equal.
However, the meanings and intentions of the various gateways of practice differ.
The eightfold right path pertains to the path of seeing,
and the path of seeing is swift.
Because the mind of diligence is swift and powerful,
it employs comprehensive strategies:
the seven factors of enlightenment and the path of cultivation.
The path of cultivation should be spacious and relaxed;
calming and insight must be balanced;
and mindfulness can then harmonize them both.
Therefore, these are employed to harmonize and balance śamatha and vipaśyanā; this concludes the three gates.
Next, the sequence will be discussed, as explained in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
When a practitioner loses mindfulness, afflictions arise;
only by binding the mind to wholesome objects can one leave transgressions behind.
Therefore, mindfulness is explained first.
When one fixes the mind on the correct view previously cultivated so that it becomes clear, this is called "discrimination of phenomena" (dharmapravicaya).
Therefore, this is explained next.
Diligently discriminating without abandoning [the practice] is called "diligence" (vīrya).
Therefore, they are distinguished in this sequence.
Because of diligence, afflictions diminish and the mind becomes joyful;
thus, joy is explained next.
Because the mind is joyful, the body attains pliancy and bliss;
therefore, pliancy is explained next.
Because the body experiences pliancy and bliss, the mind attains tranquil concentration.
Therefore, next, concentration is explained.
This concentration is precisely the Vajra Samādhi;
by attaining this concentration, one neither sinks nor emerges, for the mind is equanimous.
Therefore, equanimity (upekṣā) is explained next.
Furthermore, because this concentration attains the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa-phala) and eliminates sorrow,
its departure from joy is termed equanimity.
Therefore, it is discussed later.
Question: It was stated previously that wisdom (*prajñā*) is able to initiate [the process].
Therefore, among the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*), mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is taught first;
it is also that which leads to the ultimate end.
Among the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*), wisdom (*prajñā*) is the last.
Now, among the seven factors of enlightenment, the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) is wisdom (*prajñā*).
Why is it not so? Why is it placed second?
To explain:
Wisdom possesses many meanings.
There is the sense of being able to initiate [an action], as explained previously.
Furthermore, it can lead to the ultimate end,
as explained above;
wisdom serves as the master of practice.
The master must provide guidance;
therefore, mindfulness is explained first.
The master must follow along.
Therefore, diligence, joy, and so forth are explained later.
Furthermore, since wisdom arises by means of its causes,
mindfulness is clarified first.
Furthermore, it can give rise to others;
therefore, diligence, joy, and so forth are subsequently proclaimed as the seven factors of enlightenment. Thus it is.
Next, the Eightfold Noble Path is explained through a fourfold analysis.
First, a general explanation of the names.
Second, the essence of the two concentrations;
third, the threefold classification of the three trainings;
fourth, the differentiation of the three types of wisdom.
What are these names?
As for the "Eightfold Path," it begins with right view and extends through to right concentration.
These eight kinds are collectively termed the "Path" (*mārga*); because they depart from the deviant, they are called "Right" (*samyak*). Question:
Why were the preceding practices, such as the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), not all termed "Right"?
This is stated specifically;
Nāgārjuna explained that one who practices the Path and enters the Dharma fears falling into heterodoxy.
Therefore, it is necessary to discuss what is correct.
Furthermore, as these eightfold paths mark the beginning of entering the state of a noble one (ārya) and the initial turning away from heterodoxy,
it is essential to distinguish their meanings clearly.
Therefore, it is specifically termed "correct.
Such are the name and meaning; this first section is concluded.
Next is the determination of the essential substance and its attributes.
The threefold analysis of meaning:
first, a general analysis according to the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*).
These eight types constitute the general stage of seeing and serve as the specific causes for that general stage.
This is designated as a "shared name.
Within this category, the single factor of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is both the path (*mārga*) and a limb of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
Because right view constitutes the essence of the path, it is designated as the "path."
Because it constitutes the stage of comprehensive vision (*darśana-mārga*), it is called a "limb of the path" (*mārgāṅga*).
The remaining seven types are simply called "limbs of the path" but are not called the "path" itself;
because they are not the essence of the true path, they are not termed the "path."
They are called "factors of the path" (mārgāṅga) because they constitute the stage of the complete realization of the truth.
Second, when distinguished according to the eight modes of activity:
the single factor of right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) can properly be called the "path" itself, but not a "factor of the path."
Because right view constitutes the essence of the path, it is called the "path";
since its essence is distinguished from its accessories, it is not called a "limb.
The remaining seven types are simply named "limbs of the path" and are not called the "path" itself.
The meaning is as explained previously.
Regarding the third [point], the distinction in terms of the fruit:
"bodhi" (awakening) refers to the path.
These eight types serve as the causes for the Path;
they are collectively termed the "factors of the path" (*mārgāṅga*). This concludes the two sections [of the four foundations of mindfulness].
Next, the factors are divided into the three trainings (*śikṣā*).
Within this section, the three trainings are first distinguished,
followed by a discussion of their sequence.
Among these eight [factors], right speech, right action, and right livelihood constitute the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Right mindfulness and right concentration constitute the training in concentration;
right view and right thought constitute the training in wisdom.
Question:
What is the distinction among the three types within the precepts?
There are three distinct types:
first, verbal action arising from the absence of hatred and delusion is called right speech.
Bodily action arising from the distancing of hatred and delusion is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).
Bodily and verbal action arising from the distancing of greed is called right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*).
Verbal action arising from the distancing of the three poisons is called right speech (*samyag-vāc*).
Physical action arising from the distancing of the three poisons is called right action;
the distancing of the four wrong livelihoods is called right livelihood.
What is the meaning of this?
As Nāgārjuna said:
first, one must abstain from "lowly food," which means not cultivating,
compounding, or selling medicinal herbs for a livelihood in order to sustain one's life.
Second, one avoids *ūrdhvamukha-bhikṣā* (upward-facing food),
which means not seeking a livelihood by divining signs such as the auspicious or inauspicious nature of the sun, moon, and constellations.
Third, one avoids *tiryagmukha-bhikṣā* (sideways-facing food).
That is to say: not flatteringly seeking office or missions through powerful and noble patrons;
not sustaining one's life through clever speech and excessive solicitation;
and being free from the four types of "mouth-food" (living off the gifts of others).
That is to say, not practicing various incantations, divinations, calculations of good and bad fortune, painting, plastering, or other such arts and crafts for the sake of one's livelihood—
being free from these four types [of wrong livelihood] is called right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*).
Third, as Nāgārjuna has explained:
by means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), abandoning the four faults of speech is called right speech (*samyag-vāc*);
abandoning the three types of bodily misconduct is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).
Abstaining from the five types of wrong livelihood is called right livelihood.
As for the five types of wrong livelihood:
the first is to falsely manifest extraordinary and unusual characteristics in order to gain profit and offerings.
First, this is the practice of sorcery;
second, proclaiming one's own merits to seek the benefit of others;
and third, practicing divination of good and bad fortune to expound it for others.
Fourth, they raise their voices with an air of majesty to inspire awe and reverence in others in order to obtain profit.
Fifth, they speak of the gains and offerings they themselves have received to move the hearts of others;
this is precisely seeking profit through profit.
These latter four types constitute the corruption of speech.
Within the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*), right concentration is primary,
with right mindfulness serving as its support.
Within the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*), right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) is primary;
it is assisted by right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*),
and right effort (*samyag-vīrya*) serves as its general strategy.
Question: The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* divides the six perfections into the three trainings;
therein, diligence is categorized under ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Now, for what reason does this [text] comprehensively apply to the three trainings?
The explanation states:
they mutually accord with principle and mutually correspond in their equality.
However, in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the six perfections are subsumed under three meanings,
wherein diligence is included within ethical discipline (*śīla*).
If, however, they are subsumed under four meanings, then diligence is treated separately as well.
Therefore, in the *Saṃtati-vimokṣa-sūtra*,
it is stated that the first three perfections constitute the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*),
while meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) constitutes the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*).
The training in the wisdom of *prajñā*,
and diligence as the means of penetration—
thus are the three trainings.
What is the sequence?
As stated in the *Tattvasiddhi*,
one who leaves the household life to seek the Way must first receive the precepts.
Therefore, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are clarified first.
Because the mind abides in virtue, right mindfulness and right concentration are clarified next.
From concentration, wisdom is generated.
Wisdom is of two kinds: coarse and subtle.
The coarse is the wisdom derived from hearing, which is designated as "right reflection."
The subtle is explained as right view through the cultivation of wisdom;
furthermore, the coarse pertains to the mundane world,
wherein one has not yet perceived the principle.
This is called right reflection.
That which is subtle transcends the world and is able to perceive the principle.
This is called right view.
Diligence pervades this sequence of practice, which does not follow the sequential order of the Eightfold Path. This concludes the three gateways.
Next, the Eightfold Path is analyzed according to the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).
As stated in the *Tattvasiddhi*:
right view is the wisdom of hearing;
right thought is the wisdom of reflection.
Regarding the remaining six, they are cultivated through cultivation.
Among these, one must first maintain the precepts to remain free from transgressions;
by maintaining the precepts, one attains the three factors of the path.
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood;
next, one cultivates wholesome dharmas.
In cultivating the wholesome, one must be diligent; first, one must clarify the nature of diligence.
Following the gathering of the mind through diligence, right mindfulness is now explained;
by means of mindfulness of the Dharma, one attains right concentration.
This is because the eightfold right path has many avenues and is elucidated in various different ways.
All shall remain unhurt;
it is not necessarily fixed.
Thus concludes the second section: the detailed explanation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma).
Third, there is the analysis in relation to nine factors,
as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:

"If one knows the roots, the causes, the inclusion, the increase, the mastership, the guidance, the excellence, the reality, and the finality regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, this is called the pure holy life (*brahmacarya*)."
These nine are the methods for encompassing the path.
What is their meaning?
There are four gates of explanation.
First, a classification according to mental factors that arise simultaneously;
second, a classification according to the meanings within the pure and mature practices of the supramundane;
third, a classification according to the sequential order from beginning to end in the Mahāyāna.
Fourth, the sequential classification from the small to the great.
Regarding the distinction among the mental factors that arise simultaneously:
among the nine [categories], the first eight constitute the practices of the path.
The latter one is the fruit of its path, practice, and realization.
The former eight are still the eight mental factors within the stage of the ten pervasive grounds (*daśa-vyāpaka-bhūmi*).
The names of these ten pervasive grounds are as listed above.
Excluding perception (*saṃjñā*) and memory (*smṛti*), the remaining eight are these [mental factors].
Among these eight, the fundamental one is the category of desire (*chanda*).
Desire is that which can initiate action.
Therefore, it is called a faculty (*indriya*).
It is categorized as contact (*sparśa*);
contact is able to bring about conjunction and give rise to the practice of the Path.
Therefore, it is called a cause.
This is included within the category of sensation (*vedanā*).
Sensation is able to receive phenomena.
Therefore, it is called "comprehension" (saṃgraha).
"Increase" (vṛddhi) refers to the mental factor of volition (cetanā).
Volition is able to initiate action and cause the Path to increase.
Therefore, it is said to be "increasing.
The master is mindfulness;
all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) revolve in accordance with mindfulness.
Therefore, it is said that mindfulness is the master of this;
it guides these factors of concentration.
Concentration is able to guide and lead forth supramundane noble wisdom.
Therefore, it is called the guide.
This excellence is a factor of wisdom;
it is the highest among all conditioned phenomena.
Therefore, it is called "victory.
"Reality" refers to the category of liberation;
it enables all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to be freed from falsehood.
Therefore, it is called "real. Question:
Mental factors (citta-dharma) are indeed numerous.
For what reason are only these eight discussed while the others are not mentioned?
The explanation states:
"Now, the meaning is elucidated by means of nine gates."
If one were to enumerate the numerous practices, they would be immeasurable.
Furthermore, within the latter three gateways, they may likewise be analyzed according to nine meanings;
however, these are not explicitly set forth here.
Now, let us discuss these eight.
Attaining nirvāṇa through these eight kinds is called "ultimate. This concludes the first section.
Next, we shall proceed to analyze, according to their meaning, the practice of accomplishment within the supramundane.
The first eight lines concern the cultivation of the path;
the final line concerns the fruit.
Within the first eight, the path arises based on desire.
Aspiration is the root of all these various practices;
therefore, it is called a "root. Question:
The Sūtras state that all wholesome dharmas have non-negligence as their root; why,
then, is desire now mentioned?
What is the meaning of this?
The Sūtra itself explains:
desire is the cause of birth.
This does not relinquish the cause of release;
rather, because we are now discussing the cause of arising, we merely intend to debate this point.
[The opponent] asks:
The Sūtras state that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment have the Buddha as their root;
yet now it is said to be desire.
What, then, is the meaning?
A sutra states:
"When sentient beings first come to know the dharmas of the Path, the Buddha is their fundamental basis."
If self-realization is rooted in desire,
then since this treatise discusses the supramundane practices realized by oneself,
it is for this reason that desire is declared to be the root.
Cultivation arises based on desire;
cultivation necessarily relies upon conditions.
Encountering external objects, the mind of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arises.
Therefore, it is called a cause.
Within this section, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are discussed in general;
when a preceding [moment] gives rise to a subsequent one, all such instances are termed contact (*sparśa*).
It is not merely a matter of the category of contact;
the distinctions among formations are diverse, consisting briefly of nine pairs,
as fully explained in the Sūtra.
First, due to faith, one draws near to a spiritual friend;
this is called "contact.
Second, due to drawing near to a spiritual friend, one hears the true Dharma.
This is called contact. Third,
because one hears the Dharma through the purity of body, speech,
and mind, it is called contact.
Through the purity of karma resulting from the four causes, one attains right livelihood;
this is called contact.
Through the five causes, one attains the pure precepts of the faculties based on right livelihood.
This is called contact.
Furthermore, the six causes— the purification of the faculties, ethical discipline, joy,
and dwelling in a secluded place— are called contact.
Seventh, because of delighting in tranquility, one is able to engage in skillful reflection.
Eighth, because of reflection, one attains dwelling in accordance with the Dharma.
Ninth, because of dwelling in accordance with the Dharma, one attains the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
That which can destroy immeasurable evil afflictions is called contact (*sparśa*). From contact,
sensation (*vedanā*) arises.
Because it encompasses the causes and encompasses the phenomena that are grasped,
it is called "encompassing" (*saṃgraha*).
Furthermore, it is through the conditions of grasping that various afflictions arise.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment can destroy it;
therefore, they are called "comprehension" (saṃgraha).
Through the comprehension of afflictions, the Path arises.
Therefore, by means of wholesome reflection, one diligently cultivates the Path to shatter all afflictions;
thus it is called "wholesome reflection" as a factor of increase.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment rely upon focused mindfulness to destroy all afflictions.
For this reason, mindfulness is designated as the sovereign.
Just as the fourfold army follows the will of the general,
so it is with the factors of enlightenment.
Because they all enter meditative absorption by following the primary object of their mindfulness,
they are able to skillfully discern the characteristics of all phenomena;
therefore, concentration is designated as the guide.
Among the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the wisdom that discriminates the characteristics of phenomena is supreme;
for this reason, wisdom is designated as the foremost.
Furthermore, by the power of wisdom, the afflictions are extinguished.
Just as in the world it is the fourfold army that destroys enemies,
or alternatively, a single brave and skillful warrior who can do so,
so it is with the factors of enlightenment.
Because the power of wisdom can destroy the afflictions,
it is called "supreme.
Although one may obtain the four dhyānas, supernormal powers, and bliss through the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, these cannot be called "real."
When one destroys the afflictions and realizes liberation, that alone is called "real.
Although the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment involve generating the resolve for awakening and practicing the path—
thereby attaining worldly happiness, the happiness of rebirth, the four fruits of the śramaṇa, and liberation— these are not termed "ultimate."
If one can sever the activities associated with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, this is called Great Nirvāṇa.
Such Nirvāṇa alone is termed ultimate. This concludes the two gates.
Next, regarding the Mahāyāna, we shall distinguish the stages from beginning to end.
At the very outset of the Dharma, the arising of a wholesome mind of affection and longing is precisely what is called "desire" (chanda).
Desire is termed the "root."
Because of wholesome affection and because of associating with virtuous friends,
it is called contact (*sparśa*).
Contact is termed the cause.
Because of associating with virtuous friends and hearing and receiving the true Dharma,
it is called "root-grasping.
Because of associating with virtuous friends, one is able to engage in skillful reflection.
Therefore, it is called "increase.
Because these four factors can cause the Path to grow and flourish—
namely mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom— they are termed the "predominant leaders."
By means of these three dharmas, one attains two liberations and severs craving; thus, through the severing of craving,
one attains liberation of mind,
and through the severing of ignorance, one attains liberation by wisdom.
This is what is called reality.
When these eight factors are ultimately realized as fruition, it is called nirvāṇa.
Therefore, nirvāṇa is called the ultimate. This concludes the three gates.
Next, to distinguish the progression from the small toward the great:
the arousal of the mind and leaving the household life is termed "desire.
Desire is termed the "root."
The formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman) is called "contact" (sparśa);
contact is termed the "cause" (hetu).
To receive two kinds of precepts is called "receiving";
receiving is termed "gathering."
Regarding the two types of precepts:
the first is the Prātimokṣa precept,
which prevents and guards against natural transgressions (prakṛti-sāvadya).
Second is the precept of purifying the faculties,
which involves distancing oneself from obstructive faults and cultivating the four dhyānas.
To call this "increase" refers to attaining the fruit of srotāpanna and the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin;
to call it "mindfulness" refers to these same attainments.
Mindfulness is designated as the "master.
Because within this stage one guards the mind and remains free from faults, it is called mindfulness.
It is given the name "guide" because it leads to the attainment of the state of an Anāgāmin.
Because one is able to lead toward and give rise to the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣaphala), one attains the fruit of arhatship;
this is called "superior.
Because it is superior to the preceding fruits, one attains the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.
This is called "reality.
Because the true qilin walks alone, it attains great bodhi;
this is called "ultimate."
Because the path reaches its ultimate limit,
the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*) are thus.
This concludes the end of the sixteenth fascicle of the *Dacheng yi zhang* (Treatise on the Meaning of the Mahāyāna).
